_meta.researchedFrom: Multiple current newcomer-guide sources per section, cited individually below. No government-equivalent single source exists for these four topics combined, so each section cites its own best source rather than one umbrella citation.

housing.summary: Securing a rental without Canadian credit history is common for newcomers and very possible with the right documents.
tips: Bring a valid passport plus your immigration document (work permit, study permit, or PR confirmation/COPR) — landlords want proof of legal status to rent to you.
Compensate for having no Canadian credit history with an employment letter showing income at least 2.5-3x the monthly rent, or 3-6 months of bank statements showing steady funds.
Offering extra months of rent upfront (where provincial law allows) or a Canadian co-signer/guarantor can replace a credit check entirely.
Budget total housing costs at or below roughly 35% of gross income, per Financial Consumer Agency of Canada guidance.
"Key money" or unofficial "furniture fees" charged outside a licensed agent are illegal in every province — report these to your provincial rental tribunal.

healthcare.summary: Public healthcare is run separately by each province, and most (though not all) require a waiting period before coverage starts.
tips: Ontario eliminated its waiting period in 2020 — OHIP coverage is immediate once your application is approved.
Most other provinces, including British Columbia, still require up to a 3-month wait after you establish residency before provincial coverage begins.
Apply for your provincial health card the week you arrive — the wait period is calculated from your residency start date, not your application date.

Buy private travel/newcomer health insurance to cover the gap in provinces with a waiting period; refugees and protected persons are covered immediately nationwide through the federal Interim Federal Health Program.
Provincial coverage doesn't include dental, vision, or prescription drugs by default — most residents carry separate private or employer coverage for those.

banking.summary: Major Canadian banks have dedicated newcomer programs and will open an account with far less documentation than is typically required back home.
tips: You need one primary ID (passport, PR card, or Canadian driver's licence) and one secondary ID (work/study permit, SIN card, or a card from a financial institution abroad).
A Social Insurance Number (SIN) is NOT required to open a basic chequing account — you can add it later, and it's only needed for interest-bearing accounts.

The major banks (RBC, TD, Scotiabank, BMO, CIBC) all offer newcomer packages that waive monthly fees for your first year, typically for anyone within 5 years of landing as a PR or holding a valid work/study permit.
Newcomer credit cards are available with no Canadian credit history required, usually with an initial limit of $500–$2,000 — the fastest way to start building a Canadian credit file.
Some banks (RBC, Scotiabank) let you open an account online before you even arrive in Canada.

transport.summary: Most Canadian cities run their own public transit system with a monthly pass — costs vary by city, but there's a usable national average.
tips: The national average cost of a monthly public transit pass is about CAD $103, though this varies significantly by city (Toronto and Vancouver run higher, smaller cities lower).
Most transit systems now use app-based or tap-card ticketing (e.g., Toronto's PRESTO, Vancouver's Compass Card) — set this up in your first week rather than paying per ride.
A monthly pass is usually cheaper than paying per trip if you'll be commuting regularly — check your city's transit authority website for current exact fares.
Many employers offer a pre-tax transit benefit or reimbursement — ask HR during onboarding.
